title: The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta | NOEMA
gist: Nathan Gardels argues the November 2026 Shenzhen APEC summit of Trump, Putin and Xi symbolized the replacement of the rules-based order with accommodating spheres of influence, with the US president now openly embracing Xi's and Putin's sovereignty-first views. Drawing on visits to Shenzhen since 1986, he traces China's rise from unplugged computers to a 20-million-person AI hub, its strategic tilt toward a dependent Russia, and contends technology is the issue most likely to trip the US-China Thucydides Trap — with China, absent from Yalta, now setting the agenda.

insights.claim: The November 2026 APEC summit in Shenzhen, where Trump, Putin and Xi met, mattered not for its substance but for its symbolism: it showcased a world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by mutually accommodating spheres of influence.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Treat great-power spheres-of-influence accommodation as the operating geopolitical regime; discount assets and alliances whose value rests on a rules-based order.
insights.quote: The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.
insights.locator: Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit

insights.claim: Public language at the Shenzhen summit about zones of 'civilizational values' and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law was code for Xi's and Putin's long-held views, which the American president has now openly embraced.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: US endorsement of sovereignty-over-law framing lowers the expected cost of regional coercion by great powers; raise geopolitical risk premia for states on the borders of China and Russia.

insights.claim: China, the one key power excluded from the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the post-WWII order, is now setting the agenda for the next international order, with Xi hosting the US and Russian leaders in its tech capital as the 'icing on the cake' of national rejuvenation.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Frames China as agenda-setter rather than rule-taker; expect Beijing-led institutional and standard-setting initiatives to gain traction.
insights.quote: The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

insights.claim: In 1986 Shenzhen's so-called tech hub consisted of nearly empty warehouses of dusty, unplugged desktop computers; 40 years later it is a technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China's 'Silicon Valley'.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: A reminder that early-stage Chinese industrial build-outs that look embarrassing can compound into world-class clusters; underestimating Chinese catch-up has repeatedly been a costly error.
insights.quote: What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

insights.claim: Shenzhen, home to Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD, is the center of gravity of China's AI battle with the United States.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Shenzhen-based champions are the frontline of the US-China tech contest — most exposed to both state support and US export controls/sanctions.
insights.quote: It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.
insights.locator: What seemed embarrassing at the time

insights.claim: Shenzhen was designated a special economic zone by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology; Xi Zhongxun, Xi Jinping's father and then Guangdong Party chief, visited California in 1980 seeking investment for it as a key platform of 'reform and opening up'.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Highlights how Western capital and technology seeded the competitor that now challenges US tech supremacy.

insights.claim: When Governor Jerry Brown asked visiting Vice-President Xi Jinping in 2012 whether China would help finance California's bullet train, the Chinese later offered financing terms too tough to accept — those who once came 'cup in hand' to California now held the financial upper hand.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Signals a reversal in capital power: Chinese state financing comes with hard terms, and US public infrastructure cannot count on it.
insights.quote: Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide.

insights.claim: By 2026 China had built a 30,000-mile bullet-train network across the country, while California and the US still have not built a single bullet train after decades of planning.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Concrete gauge of the state-capacity gap in infrastructure delivery; underpins Beijing's narrative of American decline and favors Chinese rail/infrastructure exporters in third markets.
insights.quote: By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

insights.claim: The author imagines a Chinese Politburo ideology chief today asserting that America, though still formidable, is 'crumbling within', its aging systems plagued by outages and unable to build even one bullet train.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Captures Beijing's perceived-decline lens on the US, which emboldens harder Chinese bargaining positions in trade and tech negotiations.
insights.quote: It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.

insights.claim: In 1986 Politburo ideology chief Hu Qili said China had cut its military by one million soldiers and was converting military plants to make refrigerators and motorcycles, while dismissing the Soviet 'polar bear' threat because Russia could not even consolidate control of Cambodia.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Shows how far China's posture has swung — from demobilization and hostility to Moscow toward military buildup and alignment with Russia.

insights.claim: After the Tiananmen crackdown in 1989, Deng Xiaoping drew a hard line on Party control, and Gorbachev's 'new thinking' has since been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for Party-state collapse to be avoided at all costs.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Political liberalization in China should be assumed off the table; economic opening coexists with an 'iron fist' on political reform.
insights.quote: Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform.

insights.claim: China's leaders came to strategically favor Putin, an autocrat obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood, over an America they see as endlessly trying to subvert China's governing system, with the 'hegemonist threat' shifting from Russia to the US even as China prospered from the US relationship.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: The Sino-Russian alignment is rooted in regime-security logic, not transactional convenience — bet on its durability rather than on a US-engineered split.

insights.claim: With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China's leaders have grown more confident in their ability to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Russia's economic dependence on China makes it a junior partner — Chinese leverage over Russian commodity flows and pricing should keep rising.

insights.claim: Bill Clinton's belief that trade would open up Chinese society, and his remark that China was on 'the wrong side of history', were wrong — and Xi and Party ideologues believe the American political class still holds that view.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Engagement-through-trade thesis is dead; policy toward China will be driven by rivalry, not convergence expectations.

insights.claim: Of all contested issues between the US and China, technology is the one most likely to trip the 'Thucydides Trap' of conflict between a rising and an established power; the Nvidia episode is just one skirmish in a larger battle.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Expect recurring export-control and chip-access shocks; semiconductor and AI-hardware names carry persistent US-China policy risk.
insights.quote: it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

insights.claim: Xi views the 'Made in China 2025' campaign, launched by Premier Li Keqiang in 2015 to conquer technologies from EVs and batteries to AI within a decade, as rocket fuel for national rejuvenation and a guard against falling behind the West as in the late Qing era.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: China's tech drive is an existential, ideological priority, so state support for EVs, batteries and AI will persist regardless of trade concessions.

insights.claim: Strategists across the US partisan spectrum see China's unrelenting push for technological goals as an existential threat to American technological supremacy and the military might and geopolitical sway it implies.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Bipartisan consensus means tech restrictions on China are durable across US administrations.

insights.claim: The author imagines Chinese leadership claiming it has shown it can go head-to-head with America on AI, has the world's largest navy and is scaling its nuclear arsenal toward parity with the US and Russia.
insights.speaker: Nathan Gardels
insights.so_what: Chinese military buildup toward nuclear parity raises long-run defense spending demand among the US and allies.
insights.quote: We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia.
